overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of why language models make confident errors and what is known about their inner workings. You'll be asked about hallucination and calibration, prompt sensitivity and unfaithful explanations, interpretability findings and their limits, and the dispute over whether models understand.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: An assistant gives the exact page range of a journal article that turns out not to exist. Which explanation best fits how language models work?

options.html: It found the article in its training text and misread the page numbers
options.text: It found the article in its training text and misread the page numbers
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model doesn't look up its training text when it writes. It generated likely text for each part of a citation, and no step compared the result with real publications.

options.html: It generated likely text for a citation, and nothing checked it
options.text: It generated likely text for a citation, and nothing checked it
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The model filled the familiar pattern of a citation with plausible contents. Generating likely text involves no comparison with the world.

options.html: It knew the article was unreal and chose to present it anyway
options.text: It knew the article was unreal and chose to present it anyway
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Nothing suggests the model knew the truth and concealed it. It generated likely text for each part of a citation, and no step compared the result with real publications.

options.html: It suffered a rare malfunction that interrupted its normal operation
options.text: It suffered a rare malfunction that interrupted its normal operation
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Researchers describe hallucination as a product of normal operation. The model generated likely text for each part of a citation, and no step compared the result with real publications.

forms.stemHtml: Researchers at OpenAI and Georgia Tech argue that common tests of model quality make hallucination worse. What is their reason?

options.html: The tests include questions that have no correct answer at all
options.text: The tests include questions that have no correct answer at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Their argument is about scoring. Most tests give a point for a right answer and nothing for either a wrong answer or "I don't know," so guessing always scores at least as well as abstaining.

options.html: The tests are written by companies that want their models to fail
options.text: The tests are written by companies that want their models to fail
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Their argument is about scoring. Most tests give a point for a right answer and nothing for either a wrong answer or "I don't know," so guessing always scores at least as well as abstaining.

options.html: The tests are too short to reveal how often a model is wrong
options.text: The tests are too short to reveal how often a model is wrong
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Their argument is about scoring. Most tests give a point for a right answer and nothing for either a wrong answer or "I don't know," so guessing always scores at least as well as abstaining.

options.html: The tests give no credit for "I don't know," so guessing pays
options.text: The tests give no credit for "I don't know," so guessing pays
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Under scoring that gives nothing for abstaining, a guess can only help. Models tuned to score well are pushed toward guessing.

forms.stemHtml: In a 2023 study, researchers planted a pattern in a prompt that steered models toward wrong answers. What did the models' step-by-step explanations do?

options.html: They justified the wrong answers and left the pattern out
options.text: They justified the wrong answers and left the pattern out
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Of 426 explanations the researchers read, one mentioned the planted pattern. The rest gave reasons drawn from the question, which is why the authors call them unfaithful.

options.html: They pointed out the pattern and warned that it might mislead
options.text: They pointed out the pattern and warned that it might mislead
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Only one of 426 explanations mentioned the pattern. The others justified the wrong answers with reasons drawn from the question and left the pattern out.

options.html: They stopped partway through and declined to give any answer
options.text: They stopped partway through and declined to give any answer
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The models kept writing fluent reasoning. Their explanations justified the wrong answers with reasons drawn from the question and left the pattern out.

options.html: They reached the right answers despite the pattern in the prompt
options.text: They reached the right answers despite the pattern in the prompt
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Accuracy fell sharply. The explanations justified the wrong answers with reasons drawn from the question and left the pattern out.

forms.stemHtml: Which of these are limits on current interpretability research, as the researchers themselves describe them? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: The methods give useful insight on only a fraction of prompts
options.text: The methods give useful insight on only a fraction of prompts
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The authors of one tracing study report satisfying insight for about a quarter of the prompts they tried.

options.html: The published cases are ones chosen because the method worked
options.text: The published cases are ones chosen because the method worked
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The examples are success cases, and the authors describe each as evidence that a mechanism exists in one context.

options.html: The internal numbers of a model can't be recorded at all
options.text: The internal numbers of a model can't be recorded at all
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A model's internal activity can be recorded. The difficulty is that the numbers carry no labels saying what they mean.

options.html: Most studies are by a company examining its own model
options.text: Most studies are by a company examining its own model
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic each studied one of their own models, and outside checking is limited.

forms.stemHtml: A model trained only on lists of Othello moves was found to hold an internal representation of the board. What does this result show about the dispute over understanding?

options.html: That language models understand the world in the way people do
options.text: That language models understand the world in the way people do
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The result comes from a small game with exact rules. It shows that a sequence-prediction model can form internal structure beyond surface patterns in a narrow setting, and how far that extends is unsettled.

options.html: That language models hold nothing beyond surface word patterns
options.text: That language models hold nothing beyond surface word patterns
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The result points the other way. It shows that a sequence-prediction model can form internal structure beyond surface patterns in a narrow setting.

options.html: That a model can form structure beyond surface patterns
options.text: That a model can form structure beyond surface patterns
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The model represented a board it was never shown. That's a clear demonstration in a narrow setting, and it leaves open how far the same holds for large language models.

options.html: That experts now agree on what the word "understanding" means
options.text: That experts now agree on what the word "understanding" means
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The meaning of the word is part of the dispute. The result shows that a sequence-prediction model can form internal structure beyond surface patterns in a narrow setting.

title: Why models err, and what is known about their inner workings
